talks.title: Powers of ten & scientific notation
talks.concept: Scientific notation
talks.launch: Solve mentally. Watch how the powers of ten behave.
talks.target: Place value with powers of ten; multiply/divide by handling the coefficients and the powers of ten separately (add exponents to multiply, subtract to divide).
anticipated: (2×10<sup>3</sup>)(4×10<sup>2</sup>) = 8 × 10<sup>5</sup> = 800,000 (multiply 2×4, ADD exponents).
(6×10<sup>5</sup>)÷(3×10<sup>2</sup>) = 2 × 10<sup>3</sup> = 2,000 (divide 6÷3, SUBTRACT exponents).
talks.record: Two columns: "coefficient" and "power of ten." Show add-exponents for ×, subtract-exponents for ÷.
moves: What happens to the exponents when you multiply? When you divide?
Why is 3.5 × 10<sup>3</sup> = 3,500 and not 350?
Write 800,000 back in scientific notation.

talks.title: Exponent rules from patterns
talks.concept: Laws of exponents
talks.launch: Write each as a single power of 2, then find its value.
talks.target: Derive the product, power-of-a-power, and quotient rules by expanding — and make sense of why 2⁰ = 1.
anticipated: 2<sup>3</sup>·2<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>5</sup> = 32 (ADD exponents). 2<sup>3</sup>·2<sup>4</sup> = 2<sup>7</sup> = 128.
(2<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>6</sup> = 64 (MULTIPLY exponents). 2<sup>5</sup> ÷ 2<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 (SUBTRACT).
2<sup>0</sup> = 1 — continue the ÷2 pattern down: 8, 4, 2, 1.
talks.record: Expand one case (2<sup>3</sup>·2<sup>2</sup> = 2·2·2·2·2) to justify "add exponents." Build a ÷2 ladder down to 2<sup>0</sup> = 1.
moves: Why ADD exponents to multiply, but MULTIPLY them for a power of a power?
Prove 2<sup>5</sup> ÷ 2<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>3</sup> by expanding.
Convince a skeptic that 2<sup>0</sup> = 1.

talks.title: Slope as rate of change
talks.concept: Slope / rate of change
talks.launch: A candle burns at a steady rate: 12 cm tall at the start, 10 cm after 1 hour.
talks.target: Interpret slope as a constant rate of change (−2 cm/hr) and use it to extend a linear relationship.
anticipated: It drops 2 cm each hour. 2 hr → 8 cm; 4 hr → 4 cm.
Slope = −2 cm/hr (it's going down). Equation: height = 12 − 2t.
Some notice it reaches 0 cm at 6 hours.
talks.record: Table of (hr, cm). Show the repeated −2. Write y = 12 − 2t and mark slope = −2.
moves: Why is the slope negative here?
Where is the "−2" in the table and in a graph?
When does the candle reach 0? How do you know?

talks.title: Solve by structure
talks.concept: Linear equations
talks.launch: Solve each for x in your head. Use the one before to help.
talks.target: Undo operations in reverse order; notice how a changing constant shifts the solution; make sense of a non-whole/negative answer.
anticipated: 2(x+5) = 30 → x + 5 = 15 → x = 10 (or distribute first).
2x + 5 = 4 → 2x = −1 → x = −0.5.
talks.record: Show the "undo" flow: subtract 5, divide by 2. For 2(x+5)=30, show BOTH distribute-first and divide-first paths.
moves: What did adding 5 to the right side do to x?
Two paths for 2(x+5)=30 — which is faster?
How can x be negative here? Does it still check out?

talks.title: Square roots between whole numbers
talks.concept: Estimating roots
talks.launch: No calculator. Between which two whole numbers does each fall — and which is it closer to?
talks.target: Anchor each root between perfect squares, then estimate to the nearest tenth by how close it sits to each.
anticipated: √16 = 4, √25 = 5 (perfect squares).
√20 is between 4 and 5, close to 4.5 (since 4.5<sup>2</sup> = 20.25).
√50 is between 7 and 8, close to 7 (7<sup>2</sup>=49) → ≈ 7.1. √8 ≈ 2.8.
talks.record: Draw a number line with perfect squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49. Drop each root between its neighbors.
moves: Which two perfect squares trap √20?
Is √20 closer to 4 or 5? How can you tell without a calculator?
Which of these are irrational? Why?

talks.title: Equivalent linear expressions
talks.concept: Distributive property & equivalence
talks.launch: Simplify or expand each. Which ones turn out equal?
talks.target: Recognize multiple equivalent forms of one linear expression — and spot the impostor.
anticipated: 3(2x−4) = 6x−12. 2(3x−6) = 6x−12. 6(x−2) = 6x−12 — all equal.
6x − 4 is the odd one out (its constant is −4, not −12).
talks.record: Expand each into standard form in a column. Box the three that match; flag the impostor.
moves: Which three are the same? Prove it by substituting x = 2.
What makes 6x − 4 different?
How many ways can you factor 6x − 12?

talks.title: Linear or not?
talks.concept: Linear functions & growth
talks.launch: Steps 1, 2, and 3 are shown. Find Step 5 and the rule. Is the growth linear — how do you know?
talks.svgHtml:
Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
talks.target: A constant first difference means linear. Express the rule (3n + 1) and connect the "+3" to slope.
anticipated: It adds 3 each step → Step 4 = 13, Step 5 = 16. Rule: 3n + 1.
It's linear because it grows by the SAME amount (3) every step — that "+3" is the slope.
If the growth changed each step (like 1, 4, 9), it would NOT be linear.
talks.record: Table of (step, tiles). Show the constant +3 difference. Write y = 3n + 1; label 3 as slope, 1 as the starter.
moves: What is the first difference between steps? Is it constant?
Where is the slope in the picture?
What would make a pattern NOT linear?

talks.title: Negative and zero exponents
talks.concept: Integer exponents
talks.launch: Continue the halving pattern. What do the negative exponents mean?
talks.target: Extend the ÷2 pattern below zero: 2⁰ = 1, then negative exponents give reciprocals (2⁻¹ = ½).
anticipated: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8, 2<sup>1</sup> = 2, 2<sup>0</sup> = 1 (keep dividing by 2).
2<sup>−1</sup> = ½, 2<sup>−3</sup> = ⅛ (= 1 ÷ 2<sup>3</sup>).
talks.record: A vertical ladder: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 → ½ → ¼ → ⅛, each step ÷2, with exponents 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3.
moves: What operation moves you DOWN the ladder?
What does a negative exponent do to the base?
Is 2<sup>−3</sup> a negative number? Why not?

talks.title: Proportional or not?
talks.concept: Proportional relationships
talks.launch: Test each for a proportional relationship (y = kx). Compute the ratio y/x as you go.
talks.target: Proportional means a CONSTANT ratio y/x and the line passes through (0, 0). y = 3x is proportional; y = 3x + 1 is not.
anticipated: (2,5): 2.5. (4,9): 2.25 — NOT constant → not proportional (it's y = 2x + 1).
y = 3x + 1 is not proportional: the "+1" misses the origin.
talks.record: For each point, compute y/x. Test the origin. Write the equation and label it proportional or not.
moves: What ratio must stay constant for a proportional relationship?
Why does y = 3x + 1 fail the test?
How could you tell from a graph in one glance?

talks.title: Tilted square — find the area
talks.concept: Area on a grid & the Pythagorean idea
talks.launch: This tilted square sits on a grid. What is its area? Then estimate the length of one side.
talks.svgHtml: <svg viewBox="0 0 206 182" class="nt-svg" style="max-height:260px"><line x1="34" y1="22" x2="172" y2="22" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="34" y1="22" x2="34" y2="160" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="34" y1="68" x2="172" y2="68" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="80" y1="22" x2="80" y2="160" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="34" y1="114" x2="172" y2="114" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="126" y1="22" x2="126" y2="160" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="34" y1="160" x2="172" y2="160" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="172" y1="22" x2="172" y2="160" stroke="#e4e8ef" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="34" y="22" width="138" height="138" fill="none" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polygon points="80,22 172,68 126,160 34,114" fill="#dcfce7" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="80" cy="22" r="4.5" fill="#16a34a"/><circle cx="172" cy="68" r="4.5" fill="#16a34a"/><circle cx="126" cy="160" r="4.5" fill="#16a34a"/><circle cx="34" cy="114" r="4.5" fill="#16a34a"/></svg>
talks.target: Find the area by boxing it in and subtracting the 4 corner triangles; connect area to side length via side = √area (the seed of the Pythagorean Theorem).
anticipated: Surround it with a 3×3 square (area 9) and subtract 4 corner right triangles (each ½·1·2 = 1) → 9 − 4 = 5.
So the area is 5 square units.
Side length = √5 ≈ 2.2 (between 2 and 3).
talks.record: Draw the surrounding square; shade the 4 right triangles; show 9 − 4(1) = 5. Then s = √5 ≈ 2.2.
moves: What is the area of each corner triangle?
How is the side length related to the area?
Between which two whole numbers is the side? Closer to which?

talks.title: One, none, or all?
talks.concept: Number of solutions of a linear equation
talks.launch: Solve each one mentally. Decide: one solution, no solution, or infinitely many?
talks.target: When the variables cancel, look at what is left: a true statement (like 4 = 4) means infinitely many solutions; a false one (like 4 = 7) means no solution; if the variable survives, there is exactly one solution.
anticipated: 2x = 10 gives x = 5, one solution.
x + 4 = x + 4: subtract x, get 4 = 4 — always true, infinitely many.
x + 4 = x + 7: subtract x, get 4 = 7 — never true, no solution. 3x + 1 = x + 7 gives 2x = 6, x = 3.
talks.record: For each, show the step where x either cancels or survives, and label it: one / none / infinite.
moves: What happened to the variable in the ones with no solution?
Both sides of the last one are equal for every x — how can you tell before solving?
Which of these could you rewrite to make the answer obvious?

talks.title: Function or not?
talks.concept: Deciding if a relation is a function
talks.launch: For each set of (x, y) pairs, decide: is it a function? Each input gets only one output.
talks.target: Scan the x-values (inputs). If any x repeats with a different y, it is not a function. Repeated y-values are fine — only repeated inputs break the rule.
anticipated: First set: inputs 1, 2, 3 all different — function.
Second set: same y = 5 three times, but inputs 0, 1, 2 differ — still a function.
Third set: input 1 goes to both 2 and 3 — not a function. Fourth: input 4 goes to 1 and 2 — not a function.
talks.record: Circle the x-values in each set so students watch for a repeat.
moves: Why is a repeated y OK but a repeated x not?
Which pair broke the third set — point to it.
Could you add one pair to the first set and ruin it? What would you add?

talks.title: Reading the shape
talks.concept: Describing graphs of functions qualitatively
talks.launch: Picture each graph in your head. Describe what y is doing as x increases.
problems: A line that rises steadily from left to right.
A line that falls from left to right.
A curve that rises slowly, then rises faster and faster.
A graph that rises to a peak, then comes back down.
talks.target: Read left to right and describe the trend: increasing, decreasing, or constant — and whether the rate is steady or changing.
anticipated: Rising line: y increases at a constant rate; decreasing line: y decreases steadily.
Horizontal line: y stays constant no matter what x does.
Rising faster and faster: increasing, but the rate itself is growing (getting steeper).
talks.record: Sketch a quick thumbnail of each described graph next to the words students use (increasing / constant / decreasing / steeper).
moves: What is the difference between 'increasing' and 'increasing faster'?
Which of these is linear, and how do you know?
For the peak graph, describe the two parts separately.
answers: increasing, and the rate is getting steeper

talks.title: Whose rate is bigger?
talks.concept: Comparing two linear functions across representations
talks.launch: Find the rate of change (slope) for each, then compare.
problems: Which climbs faster: y = 3x + 2 or the table above?
Which starts higher (bigger y-intercept): y = 2x + 5 or y = 2x + 1?
Line A goes up 4 for every 1 right; Line B is y = 5x. Steeper?
talks.target: Pull the slope out of each form — the coefficient of x in an equation, or the change in y per step of x in a table — then compare those numbers directly.
anticipated: y = 3x + 2 has slope 3; the table goes up 3 each step, so slope 3 too — they tie.
y-intercepts: 5 versus 1, so y = 2x + 5 starts higher.
Line A slope 4, Line B slope 5 — B is steeper.
talks.record: Build a two-column compare chart: slope and y-intercept for each function, pulled from whatever form it came in.
moves: Where did you find the slope in the table versus in the equation?
Two functions can tie on slope — what still makes them different?
Does a bigger y-intercept mean the line is steeper?

talks.title: Where do they cross?
talks.concept: Solutions of a system as an intersection point
talks.launch: Each pair of lines is a system. Find where they cross — or decide if they never do.
talks.target: The solution is the point that satisfies both lines. Substitute one into the other in your head; parallel lines (same slope, different intercept) never meet, so there is no solution.
anticipated: y = x and y = 4: the point where x = 4 gives (4, 4).
y = x and y = −x cross where x = −x, so x = 0: the point (0, 0).
y = x + 1 and y = x + 3 are parallel — no solution. y = 2x and y = x + 1: 2x = x + 1, x = 1, point (1, 2).
talks.record: Sketch each pair on a quick grid and mark the crossing point (or note 'parallel — none').
moves: How could you tell two lines never cross without graphing?
For y = 3 and x = 5, what point sits on both?
Check (1, 2) in both equations of the fourth system — does it fit?

talks.title: Rational or not?
talks.concept: Rational versus irrational numbers
talks.launch: Decide if each number is rational (a ratio of integers, ending or repeating decimal) or irrational.
talks.target: A number is rational if it can be written as a fraction of integers — this includes terminating and repeating decimals. Non-repeating, non-terminating decimals (and roots of non-perfect-squares) are irrational.
anticipated: 0.75 = 3/4, rational; √9 = 3, a whole number, rational.
0.333... = 1/3, repeating, so rational.
√2 = 1.414... never repeats — irrational; π = 3.1415... never repeats — irrational.
talks.record: Two columns, rational and irrational; write each number under its column with its fraction form when it has one.
moves: A repeating decimal looks endless — why is it still rational?
√9 is irrational-looking but isn't — what makes the difference?
How is √2 different from √9?

talks.title: Temperature swings
talks.concept: Multi-step problems with rational numbers
talks.launch: Work each step in your head, watching the signs carefully.
problems: It is −5°. It warms 8°. New temperature?
From 4°, it drops 3° each hour for 2 hours. New temperature?
A diver at −12 m rises 5 m, then rises 3 m more. Depth now?
Your account is −$6. You add $10, then spend $2. Balance?
Start at 0. Add 12, then subtract 14. Result?
talks.target: Break each situation into ordered steps, applying one operation at a time and tracking the sign of the running total.
anticipated: −5 + 8 = 3°.
4 − 3(2) = 4 − 6 = −2°.
−12 + 5 + 3 = −4 m; −6 + 10 − 2 = 2 dollars; 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4.
talks.record: Write each running total after every step so the sign changes are visible.
moves: Which step flipped the number from negative to positive?
Could you combine the two hourly drops into one move?
How is 'drops 3 each hour for 2 hours' the same as multiplying?

talks.title: Move the point
talks.concept: Transformations of a point on the coordinate plane
talks.launch: Transform the point in your head. Say the new coordinates.
talks.target: Each transformation has a coordinate rule: reflect over x-axis negates y; over y-axis negates x; translate adds to each coordinate; a 180° rotation about the origin negates both.
anticipated: Over the x-axis, the y flips sign: (3, 4) → (3, −4). Over the y-axis, x flips: (3, 4) → (−3, 4).
Translate right 3, up 2: add to each — (2 + 3, 1 + 2) = (5, 3).
180° about origin negates both: (1, 2) → (−1, −2).
talks.record: List the rule beside each result: (x, −y), (−x, y), (x + a, y + b), (−x, −y).
moves: Which coordinate changed when you reflected over the x-axis, and why?
How is a 180° rotation like doing two reflections?
Translating never changes signs — so what does it change?

talks.title: Volumes with π ≈ 3
talks.concept: Volume of cylinders, cones, spheres, and pyramids
talks.launch: Use π ≈ 3 to estimate each volume mentally.
problems: Cone with the same r = 2, h = 3. Volume ≈?
talks.target: Substitute π ≈ 3 to keep numbers friendly. Remember a cone is one-third of its matching cylinder, and a pyramid is one-third of base area times height.
anticipated: Cylinder: 3 × 4 × 3 = 36; the cone is one-third of that, so 12.
talks.record: Chart the cylinder and its cone side by side so the one-third relationship stands out.
moves: Why is the cone exactly a third of the cylinder?
How did π ≈ 3 make the sphere calculation friendly?
Which formula also uses one-third besides the cone?

talks.title: Reading a scatter cloud
talks.concept: Association and outliers in scatter plots
talks.launch: Picture each scatter plot. Describe the association and spot anything unusual.
problems: Points drift up to the right. Positive or negative association?
Points drift down to the right. Which association?
Points scattered with no trend. Association?
A tight up-right band with one point far below. What is that point?
Points hug a straight up-right line closely. Strong or weak?
talks.target: Read the overall direction (up-right is positive, down-right is negative, no direction is none), judge how tightly points cluster to a line for strength, and flag any point that sits far from the pattern as an outlier.
anticipated: Up to the right means as x grows, y grows — positive association.
Down to the right is negative; no trend means no association.
The lone point far from the band is an outlier; points tight to a line show strong association.
talks.record: Sketch each described cloud and label direction, strength, and any outlier.
moves: What is the difference between 'no association' and 'negative association'?
How do you decide if an association is strong or weak?
Where exactly is the outlier, and how far off is it?

talks.title: Predict with the line
talks.concept: Using a linear model to predict and interpret
talks.launch: A taxi charges cost = 2m + 3 dollars for m miles. Use the model in your head.
problems: What does the 3 mean in cost = 2m + 3?
One ride cost $13. About how many miles?
talks.target: In cost = 2m + 3, the y-intercept 3 is the starting fee at zero miles and the slope 2 is the added cost per mile. Substitute a value of m to predict, or work backward from a cost.
anticipated: The 3 is the flat fee before you move; the 2 is dollars per mile.
$13 means 2m + 3 = 13, so 2m = 10, m = 5 miles.
talks.record: Label the equation: 3 = start-up (y-intercept), 2 = per-mile rate (slope); then chart cost at 5 and 10 miles.
moves: Which number is the slope, and what real thing does it measure?
How did you undo the model to find the miles from the cost?
What would the graph's line hit on the cost axis at 0 miles?

talks.title: Compound chances
talks.concept: Probabilities of compound events from sample spaces
talks.launch: Find each probability as a simple fraction. Think about the whole sample space.
problems: One die: P(rolling an even number)?
Coin and die: P(heads and a 6)?
Two coins: P(at least one head)?
talks.target: List or picture all equally likely outcomes, then count the favorable ones over the total. For independent stages, multiply the single-stage probabilities.
anticipated: P(heads) = 1/2; a die has 3 evens out of 6, so 1/2.
Two coins have 4 outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT); both heads is 1 of 4 = 1/4.
Heads and a 6: (1/2)(1/6) = 1/12; at least one head is 3 of the 4 outcomes = 3/4.
talks.record: List the 4-outcome sample space for two coins so students can count directly.
moves: How did listing all outcomes help with 'at least one head'?
Why can you multiply for 'heads and a 6'?
What is the total number of outcomes for a coin and a die together?

talks.title: Complements and combinations
talks.concept: Complementary and independent compound events
talks.launch: Reason about each event mentally. Watch for complements and for independent stages.
problems: P(drawing a red) = 14. P(not red)?
Flip two fair coins: P(both tails)?
Spin a spinner P(win) = 13 twice: P(win both)?
Roll a die: P(a 4 or a 5)?
talks.target: A complement subtracts the event's probability from 1. For independent events happening together, multiply. Mutually exclusive 'or' events add their probabilities.
anticipated: P(no rain) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7; P(not red) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
A 4 or a 5 are exclusive, so 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.
talks.record: Split the board: 'complement (1 − P)' on one side, 'independent (multiply)' on the other; place each problem under its rule.
moves: When do you subtract from 1 instead of multiplying?
Why do the two coin flips multiply rather than add?
How is 'a 4 or a 5' different from 'a 4 and then a 5'?

talks.title: Counting the ways
talks.concept: The multiplication counting principle
talks.launch: Count the total number of ways by multiplying the choices at each stage.
problems: 3 shirts and 4 pants: how many outfits?
2 breads and 3 fillings: how many sandwiches?
Flip a coin 3 times: how many outcomes?
3 appetizers, 2 mains, 2 desserts: how many meals?
A 2-digit code using digits 1–5 (repeats allowed): how many?
talks.target: When independent choices combine, multiply the number of options at each stage to get the total count of outcomes.
anticipated: 3 shirts × 4 pants = 12 outfits; 2 × 3 = 6 sandwiches.
Coin 3 times: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes.
Meals: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12; code: 5 × 5 = 25.
talks.record: Write each as a multiplication chain (options × options × ...) with the product circled.
moves: Why do you multiply the stages instead of adding them?
How does flipping a coin 3 times become 2 × 2 × 2?
What changes in the code count if repeats were not allowed?

talks.title: Legs first, then the diagonal
talks.concept: Distance between two points as the hypotenuse of a right triangle
talks.launch: Between two points, the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs. Find each leg, then use the Pythagorean theorem for the straight-line distance.
talks.target: Read the two legs off the coordinates (difference in x, difference in y), then combine with a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup>. Friendly triples (3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13) make the diagonal come out whole.
anticipated: The legs 3 and 4 give 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5.
For (0,0) to (6,8): legs 6 and 8, 36 + 64 = 100, distance 10.
Last one: legs are 13 − 1 = 12 and 7 − 2 = 5, so √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13.
talks.record: Sketch each right triangle with the horizontal leg, vertical leg, and dashed hypotenuse labeled; write a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup> underneath so the legs-to-diagonal move is visible.
moves: How did you get each leg without plotting the points?
Where do you see 3-4-5 hiding inside the third problem?
Which subtraction gave the horizontal leg, and which gave the vertical leg?

talks.title: Ladders, screens, and ramps
talks.concept: Pythagorean theorem in design and measurement problems
talks.launch: Each situation hides a right triangle. Name the two legs, then find the missing distance.
problems: A ladder's base sits 3 ft from a wall and reaches 4 ft up. How long is the ladder?
A TV screen is 6 in tall and 8 in wide. How long is its diagonal?
A ramp rises 5 ft over a run of 12 ft. How long is the ramp surface?
A wire runs from the top of a 9 ft pole to a stake 12 ft away on the ground. How long is the wire?
A rectangular field is 8 m by 15 m. How far is the diagonal walk across it?
talks.target: Translate each design into legs and a hypotenuse, then apply a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup>. The numbers are chosen so the answer is a whole measurement.
anticipated: Ladder: 3 and 4 are legs, so the ladder is the hypotenuse, 5 ft.
Pole and wire: 9 and 12 give 81 + 144 = 225, √225 = 15 ft.
Field: 8 and 15 give 64 + 225 = 289, √289 = 17 m.
talks.record: For each problem draw the object, mark the two known legs with their units, and put a question mark on the hypotenuse being found.
moves: In each story, which measurement is the hypotenuse and how do you know?
Which of these use the same triple you already knew?
How would the ladder answer change if the base were 6 ft and the height 8 ft?

talks.title: Undo to isolate the letter
talks.concept: Solving a formula for one of its variables
talks.launch: Treat the target variable like the unknown in any equation: undo whatever is attached to it. Solve each formula for the requested letter.
problems: Solve y = mx + b for x
talks.target: The same inverse-operation moves that solve numeric equations rearrange a formula. Divide off a factor, or subtract then divide, to leave the target variable alone.
anticipated: In d = rt, t is multiplied by r, so divide both sides by r: t = d/r.
P = 4s divides by 4 to give s = P/4; C = 2πr divides by 2π to give r = C/(2π).
y = mx + b needs two undos: subtract b first, then divide by m, so x = (y − b)/m.
talks.record: Write each formula with the target variable circled, then show the single divide (or subtract-then-divide) that isolates it beside the result.
moves: What operation is attached to the letter we want, and what undoes it?
Which formula needed two steps instead of one, and why?
How is solving A = lw for w the same as solving 12 = 3w for w?

talks.title: Rise over run off the grid
talks.concept: Reading slope from a graph as rise divided by run
talks.launch: Slope is the rise divided by the run between two points on the line. Find each slope; watch the sign and the flat case.
problems: A line passes through (0, 0) and (2, 6). What is its slope?
A line passes through (0, 1) and (4, 3). What is its slope?
A line drops 2 units for every 1 unit right. What is its slope?
A line passes through (1, 2) and (5, 2). What is its slope?
A line rises 3 for a run of 6. What is its slope?
talks.target: Count the vertical change (rise) and horizontal change (run) between two lattice points, then form the ratio. A drop makes the slope negative; a flat line makes it 0.
anticipated: (0,0) to (2,6): rise 6, run 2, slope 6/2 = 3.
Dropping 2 for every 1 right means rise −2 over run 1, slope −2.
(1,2) to (5,2): the y-values never change, so rise 0 and slope 0.
talks.record: On a sketched grid, draw the rise as a vertical arrow and the run as a horizontal arrow between the two points, and write the fraction rise/run next to each.
moves: How do you decide which change is the rise and which is the run?
What in the third problem makes the slope negative?
Why does the horizontal line come out to 0 instead of undefined?

talks.title: Spot m, spot b
talks.concept: Reading and building equations in y = mx + b form
talks.launch: In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. Read the parts, then evaluate and build.
problems: In y = 3x + 2, what is the y-intercept?
In y = 3x + 2, what is the slope?
For y = 3x + 2, find y when x = 0.
For y = 2x + 1, find y when x = 4.
Write the equation with slope 5 and y-intercept −3.
talks.target: The number multiplying x is the slope; the constant is the y-intercept and the value of y at x = 0. Reverse the reading to write an equation from a given slope and intercept.
anticipated: In y = 3x + 2 the slope is 3 and the intercept is 2; at x = 0, y = 2.
For y = 2x + 1 at x = 4: 2×4 + 1 = 9.
Slope 5, intercept −3 builds y = 5x − 3.
talks.record: Above one equation, label the m-slot and the b-slot; keep a two-column chart of 'slope' and 'y-intercept' as students name each part.
moves: Why does finding y at x = 0 always give you b?
How did you place the −3 when writing the last equation?
Which part of the equation tells you how steep the line is?

talks.title: Two points make a line
talks.concept: Building a linear equation from two observed points
talks.launch: Any two points give you a slope, and the slope plus one point gives the whole equation. Work up to writing y = mx + b.
problems: Write the equation of the line through (0, 4) with slope 3.
Write the equation of the line through (1, 3) and (2, 5).
talks.target: Find slope as the change in y over the change in x, then use the y-intercept (or back-substitute a point) to finish y = mx + b. Equal y-values signal a slope of 0.
anticipated: (1,3) to (2,5): rise 2, run 1, slope 2.
The point (0, 4) IS the y-intercept, so with slope 3 you get y = 3x + 4 directly.
For (1,3) and (2,5): slope 2, and substituting (1,3) gives b = 1, so y = 2x + 1.
talks.record: Write the slope fraction (Δy over Δx) between the two points, then show the substitution that pins down b before writing the final equation.
moves: When is one of the given points already the y-intercept?
How did you find b once you had the slope?
What does a slope of 0 tell you about those two points?

talks.title: Start-up plus a steady rate
talks.concept: Modeling real situations with y = mx + b and predicting
talks.launch: A gym charges $20 to join plus $10 each month. Find the pieces of the model, then use it to predict.
problems: What is the total cost after 3 months?
Which amount is the one-time start-up fee (the b)?
Which amount is the rate per month (the m)?
Write the model for cost C after m months.
talks.target: The fixed start-up cost is the y-intercept b and the per-month charge is the slope m, giving C = 10m + 20. Substitute a month value to predict any future cost.
anticipated: After 3 months: 20 + 3×10 = 50 dollars.
The $20 is paid once, so it is b; the $10 repeats each month, so it is m.
Model C = 10m + 20, and at m = 12: 10×12 + 20 = 140 dollars.
talks.record: Build a running table of months vs. total cost (0→20, 1→30, 2→40, 3→50) so the constant +10 and the starting 20 are visible before writing the equation.
moves: Where do you see the $20 in the table, and where do you see the $10?
How does the model let you skip straight to month 12?
What would change in the equation if joining cost $0?

talks.title: Find the rule, fill the table
talks.concept: Inferring a linear rule from a table and predicting outputs
talks.launch: Look at how y changes as x steps up by 1. That constant change is the slope; back up to x = 0 for the start. Table: x = 1,2,3 gives y = 5,7,9.
problems: As x increases by 1, how much does y increase?
What is y when x = 0 (the starting value)?
Write the rule for this table.
Use the rule to find y when x = 5.
A different table shows x = 2 → 10 and x = 3 → 15. What is its rule?
talks.target: The constant step in y per unit x is the slope; extending back to x = 0 gives the y-intercept, so the rule is y = 2x + 3. A proportional table (y = 5x) has intercept 0.
anticipated: y jumps 2 each step (5,7,9), so slope 2; backing from x = 1, y = 5 down to x = 0 gives 3.
Rule y = 2x + 3, and at x = 5: 2×5 + 3 = 13.
Second table: y is always 5 times x, so y = 5x with no constant added.
talks.record: Under the table, write the +2 steps between consecutive y-values, then extend the table left to x = 0 to expose the intercept before writing the rule.
moves: How did the constant difference help you find the slope?
How did you get back to the x = 0 value the table didn't show?
Why does the second table have no constant term?

talks.title: Add or subtract to erase a variable
talks.concept: Solving linear systems by elimination
talks.launch: When two equations line up, adding or subtracting them can cancel a variable. Combine the equations, then back-solve.
problems: x + y = 10 and x − y = 2. Add the equations. What does 2x equal?
Use x + y = 10 to find y.
3x + y = 17 and 2x + y = 12. Subtract to eliminate y. What is x?
Use 2x + y = 12 with x = 5 to find y.
talks.target: Choose to add when opposite terms cancel and to subtract when matching terms cancel. Solving the resulting one-variable equation, then substituting back, finds both values.
anticipated: Adding x + y and x − y cancels y, giving 2x = 12, so x = 6, then y = 4.
For the second pair, the y-terms match, so subtracting cancels y: x = 17 − 12 = 5.
Substituting x = 5 into 2x + y = 12: 10 + y = 12, so y = 2.
talks.record: Stack each pair of equations and draw the add or subtract bar beneath, showing the cancelled variable and the single-variable result before back-substituting.
moves: How did you decide to add the first pair but subtract the second?
Which variable disappears in each step, and why?
Once you know x, which equation is easiest for finding y?

talks.title: One, none, or infinitely many
talks.concept: Classifying systems by number of solutions
talks.launch: Compare slopes and intercepts. Same slope and same intercept is one line; same slope, different intercept never meets; different slopes cross once. Classify each pair.
problems: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x + 5. How many solutions?
y = 3x + 4 and y = 3x + 4. How many solutions?
y = 2x + 1 and y = 3x − 1. How many solutions?
Two lines have the same slope and the same y-intercept. How many solutions?
Two lines are parallel with different y-intercepts. How many solutions?
talks.target: Different slopes guarantee exactly one intersection; identical equations are the same line with infinitely many solutions; equal slopes with different intercepts are parallel and have none.
anticipated: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x + 5 share slope 2 but differ in intercept, so they are parallel: no solution.
The identical equations describe one line, so every point works: infinitely many.
Slopes 2 and 3 differ, so the lines cross exactly once: one solution.
talks.record: Make a three-column chart headed 'one / none / infinite' and sort each pair into a column based on its slope-and-intercept comparison.
moves: Which comparison do you check first, slope or intercept?
How can two equations look different but still be the same line?
What has to be true for a system to have no solution at all?
